title: Percent on receipts, and prove it
summary: Turn percents into fractions and decimals on real prices, then write your first proofs using a two way check.
materials: a real receipt or store ad, if you have one

problems.prompt: What is 599 + 246?
explanation: Round 599 up to 600 first, since that is only 1 away.
You added 1 too many, so subtract it back: 846 - 1 is 845.
problems.useAgain: when one of the numbers you are adding is close to a round number.
hints: 599 is only 1 away from a round number.
Add the round number first, then take the extra back off.
problems.socraticHint: Rounding always shifts the numbers a little before you add them. Once you round 599 up, what do you owe your final total to make it exactly right again?

problems.prompt: What is 5000 - 486?
explanation: Round 486 up to 500, since that is easier to subtract.
You subtracted 14 too many, so add 14 back: 4500 + 14 is 4514.
problems.useAgain: when the number you are subtracting is close to a round number.
hints: 486 is close to 500.
Subtract the round number first, then add back what you subtracted too much.
problems.socraticHint: This time it is the number you are subtracting that gets rounded, not the number you start with. Does that change whether you owe your answer more or less at the end?

problems.prompt: A $45 shirt is discounted by 20%, then an additional 10% is taken off the discounted price. What is the final price?
explanation: 20% off $45 multiplies by 0.8: 45 x 0.8 is $36.
An additional 10% off that new $36 multiplies by 0.9: 36 x 0.9 is $32.40.
The two discounts do not simply add to 30%, since the second one applies to the smaller $36.
problems.useAgain: when two discounts are applied one after another, since the second discount always applies to the already-discounted price.
hints: Apply the first 20% discount completely before touching the second one.
The second discount applies to the NEW price, not the original $45.
problems.socraticHint: If you just added 20% and 10% to get 30% off the original $45, would that give the same answer as applying them one after another?

variant.prompt: A $60 jacket is discounted by 25%, then an additional 20% is taken off the discounted price. What is the final price?

problems.prompt: What is 3/5 of 40?
explanation: Of means times: 3/5 of 40 means 3/5 times 40.
Divide 40 by 5 to find one fifth, which is 8.
Multiply 8 by 3 to find three fifths, giving 24.
problems.useAgain: when you take a fraction of a whole number and can find one part before scaling it up.
hints: Divide by the bottom number first, then multiply by the top.
One fifth of 40 is a lot easier to find than three fifths all at once.
problems.socraticHint: Of means times, but multiplying by a fraction like 3/5 is really two smaller jobs done one after another. What is the first one?

problems.prompt: What is the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 50?
explanation: Pair the ends. The first and last numbers, 1 and 50, add to 51. So do 2 and 49, and every pair made the same way.
There are 50 numbers, so that makes 25 pairs, each adding to 51.
25 times 51 is 1275.
problems.useAgain: when you need to add a long run of consecutive whole numbers quickly, since pairing the first and last (and so on) always gives the same total.
hints: Do not add the numbers one at a time. Pair the first number with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on.
Every pair adds up to the same total. Multiply that pair-total by how many pairs there are.
problems.socraticHint: If you paired 1 with 50, 2 with 49, and kept going, would every single pair add up to the exact same number?

variant.prompt: What is the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 40?

problems.prompt: What is 7.2 multiplied by 100?
explanation: Multiplying by 100 is two shifts of one place each, so shift every digit two places to the left.
7.2 shifted two places: the 7 moves from ones to hundreds, the 2 moves from tenths to tens.
That gives 720.
problems.useAgain: when you multiply a decimal by 100 and want to move the point two places instead of one.
hints: Times 100 is two shifts of one place, not one big jump.
Count two places to the right of where the point starts.
problems.socraticHint: Multiplying a whole number by 100 and multiplying a decimal by 100 follow the exact same rule. What is that rule, in your own words?

problems.prompt: A jar is 3/4 full. You pour out half of what's in the jar. What fraction of the whole jar is now empty?
explanation: The jar starts 3/4 full. Pouring out half of what's inside removes half of 3/4, which is 3/8.
What's left full is 3/4 minus 3/8, which is 3/8.
Empty is the rest of the whole jar: 1 minus 3/8 is 5/8.
problems.useAgain: when you pour out a fraction of what's already in a container, not a fraction of the whole container.
hints: Find how much gets poured out first, as a fraction of the WHOLE jar, not just half.
Subtract what's still full from 1 whole to find what's empty.
problems.socraticHint: Is pouring out half of what's in a 3/4-full jar the same as pouring out half of the WHOLE jar?

variant.prompt: A jar is 5/6 full. You pour out half of what's in the jar. What fraction of the whole jar is now empty?

problems.prompt: What is 1 - 3/8?
explanation: Rewrite the whole number 1 as 8/8, the same size slice as eighths.
Now both numbers are cut into eighths, so subtract the tops: 8 - 3 is 5.
That leaves 5/8.
problems.useAgain: when you subtract a fraction from a whole number and need to rewrite the whole number as the same size slice first.
hints: Rewrite 1 as a fraction with the same bottom number as 3/8.
8/8 is the same amount as 1.
problems.socraticHint: A whole pizza, and eight out of eight slices of that same pizza. Are those two different amounts?

problems.prompt: In week 5's gear example, the wheel turns once for every 4 times the small motor gear spins. If the motor gear spins 20 times, how many times does the wheel turn?
explanation: Trade speed for strength: gears turn the wheel slower than the motor, so the wheel turns fewer times.
In that example, every 4 motor spins make 1 wheel turn, a 4 to 1 ratio.
20 motor spins divided by 4 gives 5 wheel turns.
problems.useAgain: when a gear ratio tells you how many small turns make one big turn, and you know one side.
hints: Divide the motor spins by the ratio number, not multiply.
In that example, 4 motor spins always make exactly 1 wheel turn.
problems.socraticHint: Does the wheel turning slower than the motor mean it needs more motor spins or fewer to turn once?

variant.prompt: In week 5's gear example, the wheel turns once for every 5 times the small motor gear spins. If the motor gear spins 35 times, how many times does the wheel turn?

explanationFigure.alt: A cube net folding up: drag to turn it, slide to fold it, and see which face lands opposite which.

problem.prompt: A cube net is laid out as a row of four squares, numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 from left to right, with square 5 attached above square 2 and square 6 attached below square 2. When this net is folded into a closed cube, which face ends up directly opposite face 1?
explanation: Fold it in your head, one square at a time. Picture the row of four squares curling around into a loop, like wrapping a belt around the cube's four side faces.
Square 2 stays put as one side, square 1 folds back to sit next to it, square 3 folds around to the far side. Square 4 closes the loop back next to square 1.
That loop wraps exactly around the four side faces. So the two squares that end up facing straight away from each other are always two spots apart in the row, not right next door.

Face 1 and face 3 are two spots apart in the row, so face 3 lands directly opposite face 1 exactly. Squares 5 and 6, folded from above and below square 2, become the top and bottom instead, opposite each other but not opposite face 1.
problem.useAgain: when a flat net folds into a box and you need to figure out which two faces end up on opposite sides.
hints: Picture the row of four squares curling into a loop that wraps all the way around the cube's sides, not just two of them.
The two faces that land opposite each other in that loop are always two spots apart in the row.
problem.socraticHint: Grab a strip of paper, number four squares 1 to 4, and fold it into a ring shape. Which square ends up directly behind square 1?

figure.alt: A flat cube net, not folded: a row of four squares numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 left to right, with square 5 attached above square 2 and square 6 attached below square 2.

variant.prompt: Using the same net, a row of four squares numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, with square 5 above square 2 and square 6 below square 2, which face ends up directly opposite face 4?

figure.alt: The same flat cube net, not folded: a row of four squares numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 left to right, with square 5 attached above square 2 and square 6 attached below square 2.

steps.title: Percent as fractions and decimals, on real receipts

explanationFigure.alt: A grid of 4 rows and 6 columns, 24 squares total, with 17 shaded, showing that you end up paying 17 out of 24 of the original price.

problems.prompt: A coupon says take 15% off, then take an extra 1/6 off the new price. Written as a single fraction of the ORIGINAL price, what fraction of the original price do you end up paying, in simplest form?
explanation: Percent is per hundred: 15% off means you pay 85 out of 100, or 17/20 of the original price.
An extra 1/6 off that new price means you pay 5/6 of it: 5/6 of 17/20 is (5x17)/(6x20), which is 85/120.
85/120 shrinks by 5 to 17/24, so you end up paying 17/24 of the original price.
problems.useAgain: when a percent discount and a fraction discount chain together, one after the other, on the same shrinking price.
hints: Turn the percent discount into a fraction of the original price first.
Apply the fraction discount to that NEW fraction, not to the whole original price again.
problems.socraticHint: Does taking 15% off and then 1/6 off add up to the same total discount as taking one bigger discount all at once?

variant.prompt: A coupon says take 20% off, then take an extra 1/4 off the new price. What fraction of the original price do you end up paying?

explanationFigure.alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares with 40 shaded, showing that the new check time is 40 percent of the old check time.

problems.prompt: mBot checks distance every 0.1 seconds. If the check rate speeds up so it checks every 0.04 seconds instead, the new check time is what percent of the old check time?
explanation: Percent is per hundred: divide the new time by the old time to compare them as a fraction. 0.04 divided by 0.1 is 0.4.
0.4 is 40 out of every 100, so that is 40%.
problems.useAgain: when you compare a new smaller time to an old time and need the percent the new one represents.
hints: Divide the new time by the old time, not the other way around.
Turn that decimal into a percent by reading off the hundredths.
problems.socraticHint: Is the new check time closer to half the old time, or closer to a tenth of it?

variant.prompt: If the check rate slowed down from every 0.1 seconds to every 0.15 seconds, the new check time is what percent of the old check time?

problems.prompt:
A $50 item goes up 20%, then that new price goes down 20%. Kayla found the final price like this:
Line 1: Find 20% of $50: 0.20 times 50 is $10.
Line 2: Add to get the increased price: 50 plus 10 is $60.
Line 3: Find 20% of the original $50 again: 0.20 times 50 is $10.
Line 4: Subtract: 60 minus 10 is $50, so the final price is $50.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 3 is wrong: once the price has increased to $60, the 20% decrease has to be taken of that new $60. It is not taken of the original $50.
Lines 1 and 2 correctly find the increased price: 20% of 50 is 10, and 50 plus 10 is 60.
20% of the new price, 60, is 12, not 10.
Subtract that from 60: 60 minus 12 is 48, so the final price is really $48, not $50.
problems.useAgain: when a percent change happens twice in a row and the second percent has to be taken of the new amount, not the original one.
hints: After the price goes up, has the amount you are taking a percent of changed to a new number?
Check which dollar amount the second 20% should be a percent of: the old price, or the new one.
problems.socraticHint: If a price goes up by 20% and then down by 20%, does it land back where it started, or is the second 20% worth a different amount of money than the first?

variant.prompt:
An $80 item goes down 25%, then that new price goes up 25%. Devon found the final price like this:
Line 1: Find 25% of $80: 0.25 times 80 is $20.
Line 2: Subtract: 80 minus 20 is $60.
Line 3: Find 25% of the original $80 again: 0.25 times 80 is $20.
Line 4: Add: 60 plus 20 is $80, so the final price is $80.
Which line is wrong?

explanationFigure.alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares with 75 shaded, showing that after 25 percent off, you pay 75 out of every 100 of the price, before tax is added.

problems.prompt: A game costs $40. It is 25% off this week. After the discount, the store adds 8% sales tax. What do you actually pay?
explanation: 25% means 25 out of every 100, so 25% off leaves 75 out of every 100 of the price. That is why you multiply by 0.75: 40 x 0.75.
40 x 0.75 is 30, the price after the discount.
8% sales tax means 8 out of every 100 gets added on top, so you pay 108 out of every 100 of the new price. That is why you multiply by 1.08: 30 x 1.08.
30 x 1.08 is 32.40, so that is what you actually pay. The trap is adding the 8% tax to the original $40 instead of to the $30 left after the discount.
problems.useAgain: when a price changes twice in a row, a discount then a tax, and you need to apply each percent to the new amount, not the original.
hints: Work out the discounted price first, before you think about tax at all.
Start with the discount: what fraction of the price is left after 25% off?
problems.socraticHint: The tax and the discount are both percents here. Do they both apply to the exact same starting amount?

variant.prompt: A toy costs $60. It is 20% off this week. After the discount, the store adds 5% sales tax. What do you actually pay?

explanationFigure.alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares with 18 shaded, showing that an 18 percent tip is 18 out of every 100 of the bill.

problems.prompt: A restaurant bill is $24. Which of these is an 18% tip on that bill?
explanation: Percent is per hundred: 18% means 18 out of every 100 of the bill.
18% of 24 is 0.18 times 24.
0.18 times 24 is 4.32, so that is the tip. The other choices come from tipping a slightly different percent.
problems.useAgain: when you find a tip or a fee by turning a percent into a decimal and multiplying it by the total.
hints: Turn 18% into the decimal 0.18 before you multiply.
Multiply that decimal by the total bill, not by a rounded version of it.
problems.socraticHint: If you already knew what 10% of this bill was, how could that help you reach 18% without starting the whole problem over?

variant.prompt: A restaurant bill is $32. Which of these is a 15% tip on that bill?

explanationFigure.alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares with 80 shaded, showing that the sale price you paid is 80 out of every 100 of the original price.

problems.prompt: A backpack is on sale for $36, after a 20% discount. What was the original price before the discount?
explanation: Work backwards: start at the end, the $36 you actually paid, and undo the discount instead of applying a new one.
20% off means you paid 80% of the original price, so $36 is 80% of the original.
Divide 36 by 0.8 to undo the 80%, since dividing is how you reverse a multiplication.
36 divided by 0.8 is 45, the original price.
problems.useAgain: when you know the price after a percent change and need to find the price before it, by undoing the change.
hints: Think about what percent of the original price you actually paid, not what percent you saved.
Divide the sale price by that percent as a decimal to undo the discount.
problems.socraticHint: The $36 you paid is not the whole original price. What percent of the original price does that $36 actually represent?

variant.prompt: A game console is on sale for $180, after a 25% discount. What was the original price?

explanationFigure.alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares with 21 shaded, showing that the 18 percent tip and the 3 percent service fee together are 21 out of every 100 of the same original bill.

problems.prompt: A bill is $80. You leave an 18% tip, then the restaurant charges a 3% service fee on the ORIGINAL bill (not including the tip). What is the total amount you pay?
explanation: Percent is per hundred: the tip is 18% of the $80 bill, which is 80 x 0.18, or $14.40.
The service fee is 3% of the same original $80, which is 80 x 0.03, or $2.40, since it does not include the tip.
Add all three amounts: 80 plus 14.40 plus 2.40 is $96.80.
problems.useAgain: when a bill has two separate percent add-ons, both based on the same original amount, not stacked on each other.
hints: Work out the tip and the service fee separately, both from the original $80.
Add the bill, the tip, and the fee together at the end.
problems.socraticHint: Does the service fee apply to the bill alone, or to the bill plus the tip you already added?

variant.prompt: A bill is $60. You leave a 20% tip, then the restaurant charges a 5% service fee on the ORIGINAL bill. What is the total amount you pay?

explanationFigure.alt: A 10 by 10 grid of 100 squares with 80 shaded, showing that the backup speed is 80 out of every 100, or 80 percent, of the forward speed.

problems.prompt: mBot backs away from an obstacle at speed 120, while its normal forward speed is 150. What percent of the forward speed is the backup speed?
explanation: 120 out of 150 is the fraction you need to turn into a percent.
Divide 120 by 150 to turn it into a decimal: 120 divided by 150 is 0.8.
0.8 is 80 out of every 100, so that is 80%.
problems.useAgain: when you turn a score, speed or amount out of some total into a percent.
hints: Divide the smaller speed by the bigger speed first.
Turn that decimal into a percent by reading off the hundredths.
problems.socraticHint: 120 out of 150 and some number out of 100 name the exact same amount. Which of those two is easier for you to picture?

variant.prompt: If mBot's backup speed were 135 instead of 120, what percent of the forward speed 150 would that be?

problems.prompt: 6 coins lie in a row, all showing tails. Each move, you flip exactly 2 coins of your choosing. Prove that you can reach all 6 coins showing heads, and prove that you can never reach exactly 5 heads and 1 tail.

mustMention: a way to flip pairs and reach all heads
the number of heads changes by an even amount each move
5 heads is an odd number so it can never happen

explanation: First show the easy direction: it can be done. Flip coins 1 and 2 to heads, then 3 and 4, then 5 and 6. Three moves, six coins, all heads. That target is reachable.

Now check the other direction: could you ever get stuck with exactly 5 heads and 1 tail? Every move flips exactly 2 coins, so the number of heads goes up by 2, down by 2, or stays the same. It only ever changes by an even number.
It starts at 0 heads, which is even, so no matter how many moves you make, the number of heads is always even.
5 is an odd number, so 5 heads is never reachable, no matter what you try. That is a two way check.
Show one target works by actually reaching it, and show the other is impossible by finding something, evenness, that never changes.
problems.useAgain: when a puzzle asks about two different targets, and you need to show one is reachable and prove the other one never is.
hints: Try building up to all heads two coins at a time and see if you actually get there.
Think about whether the number of heads can ever switch from even to odd, not just whether it can equal 5.
problems.socraticHint: A two way check needs two different kinds of proof for two different claims. Which kind of proof shows something is possible, and which kind shows something can never happen, no matter what you try?

problems.prompt: Invent your own puzzle that pigeonhole or a parity argument (staying odd or even) can settle, your choice. State the puzzle clearly, give the answer, then prove it the way this week's proofs do: show why the answer must always be true, not just true for the examples you tried.

mustMention: not just the cases you tried

explanation: Pigeonhole: with more of one thing than slots, for example 13 kids and only 12 birthday months, two kids must share a month.
Parity: a count that only ever moves by an even amount can never reach zero from an odd start, no matter how many moves happen.
Either way, the proof has two halves: show the situation forces the outcome, and show a smaller number does not.
Check your own puzzle against a few different starting cases, not just one, before you trust that it always holds.
problems.useAgain: when you want to build your own puzzle that pigeonhole or parity can settle, instead of only solving someone else's.
hints: Pigeonhole needs one number that is bigger than another, like more people than months. Parity needs a count that only ever moves by an even amount.
Try a small, real setup first, like socks, birthdays or coins, and see whether one of the two ideas already fits it.
problems.socraticHint: Could you build your puzzle around something you already own or do every day, instead of inventing an imaginary scenario from nothing?

problems.prompt: 20 fence posts start out painted white. Each day, exactly 4 of them get repainted to the other color, white ones turn red and red ones turn white. Prove that you can never end a day with exactly 3 posts painted red.

mustMention: red count changes by an even number each day
3 is odd so it is impossible

explanation: Count how many posts are red. At the start, all posts are white, so 0 posts are red.
Each day, exactly 4 posts get repainted: some were red and turn white, some were white and turn red. If r were red-to-white and w were white-to-red, r plus w is 4.
After the day, the red count changes by w minus r. Since r plus w is 4, an even number, w minus r is also always even.
So the red count always stays even, since it started at 0 posts. Exactly 3 red posts is an odd number, so it can never happen, no matter how many days pass.
problems.useAgain: when a fixed number of things swap between two states each round, and you want to know whether a count can ever land on an odd number.
hints: Count how many posts are red right now, not white.
Every day 4 posts get repainted total, some red-to-white and some white-to-red, and that split controls how the red count changes.
problems.socraticHint: Every day, some red posts turn white and some white posts turn red. If the same number make each of those two swaps, does the total count of red posts change at all?

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write, in your own words, why showing that a count can never change from even to odd proves a target is impossible, no matter how many moves you try.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record yourself explaining the two way check: how you proved all 6 coins showing heads was reachable, and how you proved 5 heads was impossible, and say what stayed the same the whole time.
